title: Section 4: Numerical Demonstration of Inverse Gram Matrix (IGM) Methods
text: vignette provides comprehensive, step--step numerical reproduction Section 4 (“Numerical Examples”) Yuen (2024) (“Inverse Gram Matrix Methods Prioritization Analytic Hierarchy Process: Explainability Weighted Least Squares Optimization Method”). primary objective demonstrate practical application closed-form Inverse Gram Matrix (IGM) prioritization framework—specifically Pseudo-IGM (PIGM), Normalized-IGM (eNIGM / NIGM), Lagrangian-IGM (lagrangeIGM)—two benchmark decision scenarios: Section 4.1 (Example 1): perfectly consistent \(4 \times 4\) Pairwise Reciprocal Matrix (PRM) \(A_1\), demonstrating PIGM resolves matrix singularity issue inherent earlier unshifted formulation attempts (Blankmeyer, 1987) matching Saaty’s Eigenvalue Method (SaatyEigen). Section 4.2 (Example 2): inconsistent \(6 \times 6\) PRM \(A_2\) evaluating high school selection criteria (Saaty, 1980), demonstrating exact closed-form Weighted Least Squares (WLS) prioritization without relying iterative numerical optimization algorithms (WLSopt).

code: library(igm4ahp)

title: Section 4: Numerical Demonstration of Inverse Gram Matrix (IGM) Methods
text: Consider perfectly consistent \(4 \times 4\) Pairwise Reciprocal Matrix \(A_1\) (Yuen, 2024, Section 4.1): \[A_1 = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 & 8 \\ 1/2 & 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 1/4 & 1/2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1/8 & 1/4 & 1/2 & 1 \end{pmatrix}\]
code: # Construct 4x4 Pairwise Reciprocal Matrix A1 A1 <- matrix(c(   1,   2,   4,   8,   1/2, 1,   2,   4,   1/4, 1/2, 1,   2,   1/8, 1/4, 1/2, 1 ), nrow = 4, byrow = TRUE)  rownames(A1) <- colnames(A1) <- paste0("C", 1:4) print("--- Pairwise Reciprocal Matrix A1 ---") ## [1] "--- Pairwise Reciprocal Matrix A1 ---" print(A1) ##       C1   C2  C3 C4 ## C1 1.000 2.00 4.0  8 ## C2 0.500 1.00 2.0  4 ## C3 0.250 0.50 1.0  2 ## C4 0.125 0.25 0.5  1 # Verify Consistency Ratio (CR) cr_A1 <- ConsistencyRatio(A1) cat("Consistency Ratio (CR):", cr_A1, "(Perfectly Consistent)\n") ## Consistency Ratio (CR): 0 (Perfectly Consistent)

what: 3.2. Step 1: Design Coefficient Matrix D Construction
title: Section 4: Numerical Demonstration of Inverse Gram Matrix (IGM) Methods
text: Using fullCoefficientMatrix(A1) (Algorithm 1; Yuen, 2024), construct \((4(4-1)+1) \times 4 = 13 \times 4\) design coefficient matrix \(D = \begin{bmatrix} D_e \\ e \end{bmatrix}\). first 12 rows (\(D_e\)) represent pairwise weighted differential equations (\(w_i - a_{ij} w_j = 0\)), 13th row \(e = [1, 1, 1, 1]\) represents unit simplex normalization constraint (\(\sum_{=1}^4 w_i = 1\)).

what: 3.3. Step 2 & 3: Gram Matrix G and Inverse Gram Matrix G^(-1)
title: Section 4: Numerical Demonstration of Inverse Gram Matrix (IGM) Methods
text: \(4 \times 4\) Gram matrix \(G_1 = D_1^T D_1\) constructed via matrix multiplication directly using element-wise formula (Theorem 2; Yuen, 2024): - Diagonal entries: \(g_{ii} = (n-1) + \sum_{k \neq } a_{ki}^2 + 1\) - -diagonal entries: \(g_{ij} = 1 - a_{ij} - a_{ji}\)

what: 3.4. Step 4: Unnormalized Row Sums & Closed-Form PIGM Priority Vector
title: Section 4: Numerical Demonstration of Inverse Gram Matrix (IGM) Methods
text: Theorem 1 (Yuen, 2024), unnormalized weight vector \(v = e G^{-1}\) obtained summing rows \(G_1^{-1}\): \[W = \frac{e G^{-1}}{e G^{-1} e^T} = \frac{e (D^T D)^{-1}}{e (D^T D)^{-1} e^T}\]
code:
# Compute unnormalized row sum vector v = e * G^(-1) v1 <- rowSums(G1_inv) cat("Unnormalized Row Sum Vector v:", round(v1, 4), "
") ## Unnormalized Row Sum Vector v: 0.5333 0.2667 0.1333 0.0667 cat("Sum of Row Sums (e * G^(-1) * e^T):", sum(v1), "

") ## Sum of Row Sums (e * G^(-1) * e^T): 1 # Closed-form priority vector via PIGM w_PIGM_A1 <- PIGM(A1) names(w_PIGM_A1) <- paste0("C", 1:4)  print("--- PIGM Priority Weight Vector (Section 4.1) ---") ## [1] "--- PIGM Priority Weight Vector (Section 4.1) ---" print(round(w_PIGM_A1, 4)) ##     C1     C2     C3     C4  ## 0.5333 0.2667 0.1333 0.0667 # Analytical fractions cat("
Exact Analytical Fractions:", paste(MASS::fractions(w_PIGM_A1), collapse = ", "), "
") ##  ## Exact Analytical Fractions: 8/15, 4/15, 2/15, 1/15

text: Theorem 4 (Yuen, 2024), lagrangeIGM solves augmented KKT block system \(\bar{G} \begin{bmatrix} W \\ \lambda \end{bmatrix} = q^T\): \[\bar{G} = \begin{pmatrix} C & e^T \\ e & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad \begin{bmatrix} W \\ \lambda \end{bmatrix} = q \bar{G}^{-1}\]

title: Section 5: Monte Carlo Simulation 1 — Equivalence Verification of IGM Methods
text: vignette reproduces Simulation 1 Section 5 (“Simulations Verifications”) Yuen (2024) (“Inverse Gram Matrix Methods Prioritization Analytic Hierarchy Process: Explainability Weighted Least Squares Optimization Method”). full benchmark simulation dataset 1,000,000 random Pairwise Reciprocal Matrices (PRMs) evaluated across four Inverse Gram Matrix (IGM) formulations—taking 21.94 minutes (1,316.48 seconds) 0.00% discrepancy error recorded 8 decimal places precision (\(\epsilon = 8\))—published Supplementary data 1 (Yuen, 2024) available direct download: Supplementary1.txt. primary objective Simulation 1 verify exact numerical equivalence priority weight vectors derived four IGM method formulations across massive dataset randomly generated PRMs: Pseudo-IGM (PIGM / pseudoIGM): Closed-form solution based full design matrix pseudoinverse \(W = \frac{e (D^T D)^{-1}}{e (D^T D)^{-1} e^T}\). Normalized-IGM (eNIGM(, r = r)): Element-form solution utilizing scalar shift parameter \(r \neq 0\) (e.g., \(r \[-1000, 1000] \setminus \{0\}\)). Unshifted Lagrangian-IGM (lagrangeIGM(, r = 0)): KKT system solution solving augmented block Gram matrix \(\bar{G}\) without scalar shift. Shifted Lagrangian-IGM (lagrangeIGM(, r = r)): KKT system solution using parameterized shift block \(\bar{G}_r\). Per theoretical proofs Theorems 1, 3, 4 (Yuen, 2024), four formulations represent mathematically identical representations unique global minimizer Weighted Least Squares (WLS) objective.
